title: Why Does Chili Burn at 37°C When Nothing's Hot? 🌶️
description:
Why does chili feel hot when it isn't? Capsaicin in chili peppers switches on TRPV1, the heat sensor on your tongue that normally fires above 43°C, so your brain feels burning with no real heat.

Sources:
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/how-capsaicin-led-to-the-2021-nobel-prize-in-physiology
https://theconversation.com/why-doesnt-water-help-with-spicy-food-what-about-milk-or-beer-226624

topic: Why does chili feel hot when it isn't?
script:
Chili isn't hot.
You've been fooled every single time.
Put one in the fridge,
and it still burns.
Your tongue is covered in tiny heat alarms.
They stay quiet,
until something hits about forty-three degrees Celsius,
that's a hundred and nine Fahrenheit.
But chili carries a molecule called capsaicin,
and it fits that alarm like a key.
The alarm goes off at body temperature,
and yells to your brain: this is burning!
So you even start to sweat,
but nothing's actually heating up.
Water won't save you,
capsaicin won't mix with it.
Milk's protein, casein, wraps it up,
and carries it away.
Birds don't even feel it,
so they happily eat chilis,
and spread the seeds.
What's the spiciest chili that's ever fooled you?
key_facts: Capsaicin opens TRPV1, the heat receptor that normally fires above about 43°C (109°F)
It opens at body temperature, sending the same burning signal with no temperature change
Capsaicin is hydrophobic and doesn't mix with water
Casein in milk wraps capsaicin and carries it away
Birds don't feel capsaicin and spread chili seeds
